description: We are Data Architects, a team passionate about turning NASA Earth observation data into pratical tools that helps farmers adapt to climate shifts. Combining data science, ML and Visualization, we transform satellite telemetry into clear insights to protect crop yields. Join us if you value structered execution and high impact problem solving!
summary:
Machamba Shift helps a farmer in Mozambique decide which crops to rotate over the next seasons. Instead of forecasting a future nobody can know, it replays the past: for
any point in the country it runs a daily soil water balance for nine local crops through
about 35 real growing seasons of NASA POWER data, and shows in how many of every 10 seasons
the rain was enough, fell short, or failed badly. It then compares crop rotations, recommends
one, explains why, and states what is given up. It addresses the challenge directly: it
compares rotations, reveals trade-offs, expresses risk in a farmer's own terms, and keeps
uncertainty visible, including a list of what the tool does not know. It matters because a
smallholder who plants maize every year in a place where maize ran short of water in three
seasons out of four is carrying a risk that open NASA data can show her today.
details:
Overview

The tool is a climate-informed crop rotation decision-support application designed to help farmers and agricultural extension officers in Mozambique choose more resilient three-season crop rotations.

How it works

Users select a location, describe their soil type and current crop, identify acceptable crops, and choose their priority: protecting harvests, restoring soil, maximising yield, or balancing these goals.

The tool provides:

  • Recent rainfall, temperature, wind, and soil wetness conditions.
  • Historical monthly and seasonal climate data from 1990 onwards.
  • Crop water-risk assessments showing how many out of every 10 seasons experience sufficient water, shortages, or severe failure, including worst-to-best year ranges.
  • Sowing-date comparisons for the current crop.
  • Hypothetical rainfall and temperature scenarios through interactive sliders.
  • Regional maps of normal rainfall, historical seasons, and statistically significant rainfall and temperature trends.
  • A recommended three-season crop rotation compared with continuous cropping, cereal alternation, and legume alternation, explaining two benefits and one trade-off.
  • A downloadable PDF report for offline use.

Scientific methodology

The application uses daily NASA POWER climate data, which is quality-checked before analysis. For each crop and agricultural season (1 October–30 April), it calculates a daily FAO-56 soil water balance to estimate water satisfaction and relative yield.

Seasons are classified as:

  • Water shortage: rainfall covers less than 80% of crop water requirements.
  • Severe failure: rainfall covers less than 50%.

All possible three-season rotations are evaluated based on water availability, soil nitrogen, resilience, yield, and crop diversity. Legumes contribute nitrogen, while cereals reduce it. Weights change according to farmers' priorities, and practically equivalent plans are presented as tied options.

Scientific limitations and reliability

The tool does not forecast climate. Tests at the study sites found that early-season rainfall does not reliably predict the remainder of the season (Spearman correlations: -0.09 to +0.16).

NASA POWER rainfall estimates were compared with ERA5:

  • Chókwè: moderate agreement (0.64).
  • Sussundenga: moderate agreement (0.55).
  • Gurué: no significant agreement (0.07), so results are flagged as unreliable.

All displayed values are identified as modelled, estimated, or sourced from scientific literature. Results compare alternatives but have not yet been validated against measured agricultural yields.

Example: Chókwè

A normal agricultural season receives 633 mm of rainfall, compared with 438 mm in a bad year and 874 mm in a good year. Maize experiences water shortages in 74% of analysed seasons and severe failure in 14%.

The recommended rotation is:

  1. Groundnut.
  2. Sorghum.
  3. Cowpea.

Supporting local knowledge

The tool supports, rather than replaces, farmers' decisions. It highlights factors requiring local judgement, including pests and diseases, field-specific soil conditions, seed and labour availability, market prices, and family food preferences.

Benefits and future development

The application simplifies agricultural risk communication using the measure "in how many out of every 10 seasons". Its regional maps cover Mozambique through 449 NASA POWER data cells.

Future improvements include integrating local soil data, agricultural prices and yields, additional rainfall datasets (CHIRPS or GPM IMERG), MODIS vegetation history, cyclone records, and official seasonal forecasts from Mozambique's National Institute of Meteorology (INAM).

Technology

Developed in Portuguese using Python, Streamlit, Folium/Leaflet, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, requests, PyYAML, and ReportLab. The project includes 130 automated tests that can run offline, with Ruff used for code quality.
